key_insight: A recurrent ASR system mirrors the human auditory cortex: different model layers map to distinct cortical regions and naturally encode a parallel hierarchy from acoustic → phonetic → lexical → semantic representations.
problem_solved: Determines whether modern recurrent speech models recapitulate the multilayered linguistic encoding in human auditory cortex, bridging model representations and cortical organization to test cognitive plausibility.
method: Compare neural recordings from human auditory cortex during speech perception with activations from a trained recurrent ASR model.

Perform layer-wise encoding/representational analyses (e.g., mapping correlations or explained variance) to link model layers to cortical regions and to classification of acoustic → phonetic → lexical → semantic content.
Statistical mapping and visualization to show spatial correspondence and the parallel progression of linguistic representations across model depth and cortex.
impact: Shows that recurrent ASR architectures organize linguistic information in a brain-like, hierarchically parallel way — useful for model interpretability, brain-informed architecture design, and evaluation of cognitive plausibility in speech systems.
visual_elements: Cortical surface map colored by model layer — lines/arrows linking each layer to specific auditory regions.
Layer vs. representation-type heatmap (acoustic → phonetic → lexical → semantic) showing strength of encoding per layer.
Schematic of the recurrent ASR stack annotated with which linguistic content emerges at each layer.
Bar/variance-explained chart comparing model layer predictions to neural responses across regions.
paper_title: Parallel hierarchical encoding of linguistic representations in the human auditory cortex and recurrent automatic speech recognition systems
paper_authors: Menoua Keshishian, Gavin Mischler, Samuel Thomas, Brian Kingsbury, Stephan Bickel
